Beyond Interleaving: Causal Attention Reformulations for
Generative Recommender Systems
Hailing Cheng
haicheng@linkedin.com
Linkedin Inc
Mountain View, California, USA
Abstract
Generative recommender systems (GR), exemplified by Meta’s
HSTU ranker architecture, model user behavior as a sequence gen-
eration problem by interleaving item and action tokens. While
effective, this formulation introduces fundamental limitations: it
doubles sequence length, incurs quadratic computational overhead,
and relies on implicit attention mechanisms to recover the causal
relationship that an item interaction 𝑖𝑛elicits a user action 𝑎𝑛. More-
over, interleaving heterogeneous item and action tokens forces
Transformers to disentangle semantically incompatible signals, in-
troducing attention noise and reducing representation efficiency.
This work presents a principled reformulation of generative
recommendation—specifically targeting architectures like Meta’s
HSTU as a ranker—by aligning sequence modeling with causal
structure and attention theory. We demonstrate that the interleav-
ing mechanism prevalent in current models acts as an inefficient
proxy for similarity-weighted action pooling. To address this, we
propose a structural shift that explicitly encodes the 𝑖𝑛→𝑎𝑛causal
dependency. We introduce two novel architectures,Attention-
based Late Fusion for Actions (AttnLFA)andAttention-based
Mixed Value Pooling (AttnMVP), which eliminate interleaved de-
pendencies to reduce sequence complexity by 50%. Our framework
enforces strict causal attention while preserving the expressive
power of Transformer-based sequence modeling, providing a theo-
retically grounded and computationally efficient path for generative
ranking.
AttnLFAperforms causal attention pooling over historical ac-
tions conditioned on item similarity, whereasAttnMVPfurther in-
tegrates action signals early by mixing item and action embeddings
in the Transformer value stream, progressively learning preference-
aware item representations. From an information-theoretic perspec-
tive,AttnMVPreduces attention noise by aligning the attention
space with the true causal graph of user behavior, enabling more
efficient representation learning.
We evaluate our methods on large-scale product recommenda-
tion data from a major social network. Compared with the inter-
leaved ranker baseline, AttnLFA and AttnMVP achieve consistent

1 Introduction
Generative recommender(GR) systems (e.g., Meta’s Hierarchical Se-
quential Transduction Units (HSTU) [ 19]) model user behavior as a
sequential prediction problem. These systems adopt Transformer ar-
chitectures [ 5,7,12,15,16] originally developed for large language
models (LLMs) [4, 8, 20] and formulate user action prediction as a
token generation process by interleaving item and action tokens.
Under this formulation, user actions are generated autoregressively
[3,9] following item tokens, enabling the model to naturally cap-
ture temporal dependencies in user interaction sequences. This
paradigm represents a significant departure from traditional rec-
ommendation models [ 1,11,17] and has demonstrated superior
performance over conventional deep neural networks, largely due
to its transductive learning capability and effective utilization of
long-range user histories. As a result, generative recommendation
has been widely adopted as a new modeling paradigm in industrial
recommender systems.
Despite its success, the interleaving formulation introduces fun-
damental limitations.
Semantic Heterogeneity of Tokens:In natural language, to-
kens share a common semantic space and are compositional by
nature. In contrast, recommender systems operate over fundamen-
tally heterogeneous entities: items (e.g., posts, videos, products)
and actions (e.g., click, like, share). Let 𝑖𝑛∈Idenote an item token
and𝑎𝑛∈A an action token, where IandAare disjoint semantic
spaces. Interleaving these tokens into a single sequencearXiv:2603.10369v1  [cs.IR]  11 Mar 2026

Missing Explicit Causality in Self-Attention:In our sequen-
tial framework, we model user actions through a localized causal
lens. While a user’s global state is informed by their interaction
historyH<𝑛={(𝑖𝑘,𝑎𝑘)}𝑘<𝑛, we posit that the specific action 𝑎𝑛

where the historical sequence acts as a contextual moderator rather
than a direct determinant:

Standard interleaved formulations often fail to explicitly articulate
this functional mapping, treating 𝑎𝑛and𝑖𝑛as part of a homogenous
sequence. In the standard causal self-attention mechanism:
Attn(𝑄𝑛,𝐾≤𝑛,𝑉≤𝑛)
where items and actions up to index 𝑛contribute symmetrically to
the attention computation, two primary issues arise:
•Causal Dilution:Action tokens attend to the entire histori-
cal prefix, which dilutes the direct causal dependency on 𝑖𝑛
with unrelated historical signals.
•Structural Ambiguity:Item tokens face difficulty in map-
ping specific previous actions to their corresponding items
due to the uniform distribution of attention weights across
all historical tokens.
Critically, positional encodings alone are insufficient to recover this
structure, as they encode sequence order but lack the capacity to
enforce the requisiteitem-action causal pairing.
Attention Noise Induced by Interleaving: Even if high ca-
pacity Transformer architectures are theoretically capable of ap-
proximating latent item-action correspondences, the interleaved
sequence format introduces systematic attention noise. Specifically,
once the model establishes a strong causal dependency between 𝑖𝑛−1
and𝑎𝑛−1, the subsequent token 𝑖𝑛—due to the locality-preserving
nature of Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) [ 14] or Relative At-
tention Bias (RAB) [ 13]—inherits a nearly identical attention bias
toward𝑎𝑛−1. This leads to the formation of spurious dependencies
where𝑖𝑛attends to𝑎𝑛−1with an unwarranted inductive bias, re-
gardless of their semantic or causal relevance. Such architectural
artifacts impose an unnecessary burden on subsequent layers to
’correct’ these correlations, ultimately degrading sample efficiency
and complicating the optimization landscape.𝑖0 𝑖1 𝑖2

Computational Inefficiency: Interleaving item and action to-
kens increases the effective sequence length from 𝑁to2𝑁. Because
self-attention has quadratic complexity in sequence length, this
results in approximately a4 ×increase in both memory and com-
putational cost. Such overhead is especially detrimental in long-
horizon recommendation settings, where scalability is a primary
concern. The increased sequence length substantially prolongs both
training and inference, reduces GPU utilization efficiency, and leads
to higher energy consumption, making interleaving-based formula-
tions less suitable for large-scale, production-grade systems.
In this work, we propose a new formulation for Transformer-
based generative recommender (GR) models that addresses the fun-
damental limitations of interleaved item–action sequence modeling.
We first provide an explicit interpretation of interleaving-based GR
methods, showing that they implicitly perform attention-based
aggregation over historical user actions conditioned on item repre-
sentations. Based on this observation, we reformulate GR modeling
as an attention pooling mechanism in which item embeddings are
used to construct the query and key projections, while action em-
beddings are incorporated exclusively through the value projections
under a strict causal masking scheme.
Building on this formulation, we introduce two improved Trans-
former architectures that decouple item and action representations
while preserving sequential dependency modeling. We evaluate
the proposed models on large-scale product recommendation data
collected from a major social networking platform and demonstrate
consistent improvements over interleaving-based baselines in both
recommendation accuracy and computational efficiency. After the
Transformer encoder, the item representations are discarded, and
the final action token representation is extracted. This representa-
tion is concatenated with additional late-fusion features and fed
into a task-specific prediction head, typically implemented using a
Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE) architecture [ 10], to gener-
ate predictions for the target actions associated with the current
item. The item-side features comprise content and metadata repre-
sentations associated with each item, including text embeddings,
author embeddings, item type indicators, and related attributes.
To incorporate personalization signals, we additionally include se-
lected viewer-side contextual features, such as device type. The
action features capture user feedback signals for each item, includ-
ing click, skip, dwell time, like, share, and comment, etc. In our

2 Architecture overview and attention
mechanism
Figure 3 illustrates a standard Transformer-based generative rec-
ommender (GR) architecture. Raw item features are first concate-
nated and passed through a projection network to produce item
embeddings. Similarly, action features—corresponding to multi-
task supervision signals such as click, dwell time, like, share, and
comment—are concatenated and projected into action embeddings
using a separate projection network. The resulting item and action
embeddings are then interleaved to form an input token sequence
of the form[𝑖0,𝑎0,𝑖1,𝑎1,...] , which is processed by a stack of Trans-
former layers (12 layers in our implementation).
In addition to sequence-level representations, we employ a set
of late-fusion features, primarily consisting of counting statistics.
These features are introduced to improve score calibration, which
is critical in production ranking systems where items are ordered
according to a value function that combines multiple predicted
outcomes. Stable and well-calibrated prediction scores are therefore
essential for reliable and controllable ranking behavior.
For fairness and reproducibility, we use the same feature set
across all model architectures evaluated in this paper. As feature
engineering is not the focus of this work, we omit further detailsand concentrate on architectural and modeling differences in the
subsequent sections.
We use a toy example to provide an intuitive illustration of how
the generative recommender (GR) architectures operate. As shown
in Figure 4, we consider two users with distinct preference profiles.
User A consistently exhibits positive engagement with dog-related
items and negative engagement with cat-related items, whereas
User B demonstrates the opposite behavior. Given a candidate item
belonging to either category, the task is to predict the user’s next ac-
tion and, consequently, decide whether a dog-related or cat-related
item should be presented.
Figure 4: Illustrative toy sequences for Users A and
B. The sequences demonstrate contrasting behavioral
patterns: User A consistently exhibits positive interac-
tions (e.g., "Like") with dog-related items and negative
interactions with cat-related items, while User B ex-
hibits the inverse preference profile. This highlights
the model’s task of capturing item-action dependen-
cies for future state prediction.
In a non-sequential point-wise recommendation setting without
personalization, the model would assign approximately equal prob-
ability to dog and cat items for both users, as predictions would be
driven solely by aggregate item statistics across the population. To
incorporate personalization in such settings, one must rely on hand-
crafted historical features, such as per-user like rates for dog and cat
items (e.g., 100% vs.0% for User A, and vice versa for User B). This
approach places a heavy reliance on manual feature engineering
and explicit content understanding.
In particular, accurate personalization requires the model to dis-
tinguish between fine-grained item semantics (e.g., dog versus cat).
If the content representation collapses both categories into a coarse
concept such as “animal,” the predictive signal is substantially weak-
ened. Moreover, achieving fine-grained semantic understanding
typically necessitates extensive item taxonomies and carefully engi-
neered historical statistics, which are costly to build and maintain
at scale. These limitations motivate sequence-based generative rec-
ommender models, which aim to learn such preference patterns
directly from user interaction sequences without relying on bespoke
feature engineering.
Interleaved GR architectures implicitly recover such personalized
signals by modeling user behavior as a single token sequence of the
form[𝑖0,𝑎0,𝑖1,𝑎1,...]. Within this formulation, the self-attention

for cat items. As a result, interleaving enables the model to encode

This analysis suggests that the effectiveness of interleaved GR
models stems from using self-attention as a structured pooling
operator that implicitly associates items with their corresponding
user actions via semantic similarity. However, this association is
formed only indirectly and incurs substantial overhead. By forcing
heterogeneous item and action tokens into a single sequence, the
attention mechanism must disentangle fundamentally different
semantic types, introducing spurious interactions and increasing
representational noise, while simultaneously doubling the effective
sequence length.

dislikes cats, this representation may still inherit positive signals

nomenon as attention noise, arising from indiscriminate mixing of

Prior work has sought to mitigate the infrastructure and com-
putational costs induced by interleaved generative recommender
architectures. For example, Huang et al. (2025) [ 6] propose an early-
fusion formulation in which item and action signals are embedded
into a unified feature space, and a dummy action token is injected
for the target item to prevent label leakage. While effective in re-
ducing sequence length, this approach fundamentally partitions
the user sequence into a context segment and a candidate segment.
In the context segment, actions are treated solely as input features
and cannot serve as supervision, whereas in the candidate segment,
actions are used exclusively as labels and are unavailable as features.As a result, long user histories cannot be trained end-to-end; instead,
the sequence must be artificially decomposed and processed in a
staged or progressive manner, requiring multiple training passes
and introducing additional system overhead. Moreover, the injected
dummy actions in the candidate segment differ substantially from
the real action embeddings used in the context segment, creating a
distributional mismatch. This discrepancy distorts the attention pat-
terns learned across segments and introduces an additional source
of modeling noise, potentially degrading representation quality and
convergence stability.
While Wei et al. (2025) [ 18] introduced Lagged Action Condition-
ing (LAC) to utilize (𝑎𝑛−1,𝑖𝑛)pairings as input tokens, we argue
that such transitions lack inherent semantic coherence. In typical
recommendation environments, item sequences are exogenously de-
termined, rendering the (𝑎𝑛−1,𝑖𝑛)pairing a structural artifact rather
than a valid causal transition. Despite the widespread adoption of
such interleaved formats for formal consistency, the literature lacks
a first-principles analysis of how Transformer architectures process
these synthetic dependencies and the potential noise they intro-
duce.
These limitations motivate a more principled formulation that
preserves the expressive benefits of interleaving—namely, learning
item–action associations directly from sequences—while avoiding
its representational and computational drawbacks. In the next sec-
tion, we introduce an alternative attention-based formulation that
explicitly models this dependency without interleaving tokens.
3 AttnLFA: Attention-based Late Fusion for
Action Architecture
Building on the analysis in the preceding sections, we argue that an
effective generative recommender must explicitly encode the causal
relationship that an exposed item 𝑖𝑛induces a subsequent user ac-
tion𝑎𝑛. Guided by this principle, we depart from the conventional
next-token prediction formulation of generative recommendation
and adopt a fundamentally different perspective. Our key insight
is that user actions can be modeled as a similarity-weighted ag-
gregation over historical actions: if a target item is semantically
similar to previously consumed items, then the user’s response to
the target item should resemble the actions associated with those
similar items.
Under this formulation, the recommendation problem is cast as
an item-conditioned action pooling task, where attention serves as
a structured, similarity-based pooling operator. Based on this idea,
we propose the attention-based late-fusion architecture illustrated
in Figure 5. Item embeddings and action embeddings are maintained
as separate representation streams. Item embeddings are processed
by a stack of Transformer layers to produce contextualized item
representations. The final-layer item embeddings are then used
as both Queries and Keys, while action embeddings are supplied
as Values in the attention operation, yielding an item-conditioned
pooled action representation.
To prevent label leakage, the proposed attention pooling is en-
forced under a strict causal constraint: the representation corre-
sponding to item 𝑖𝑛may attend only to items at positions {0,...,𝑛−
1}, and is explicitly prohibited from attending to its own position 𝑛.

Attention-based Late Fusion for Actions (AttnLFA).

To assess effectiveness, we compareAttnLFAagainst a strong

comparison, we maintain identical hyperparameter configurations
and architectural components—including embedding layers, Trans-

Furthermore, we employRotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE)
[14] as the universal positional encoding scheme throughout our

Encouraged by the effectiveness ofAttnLFA, we further ex-

and is expected to yield further performance gains. In practice, we
set𝜆= 1, and preliminary sensitivity analysis over 𝜆∈[ 0.5,1.0]
indicates stable performance. After𝑇(= 12) layers of Transformer
blocks, at the final layer, we apply an action pooling operation
identical toAttnLFA. This formulation enables each Transformer
layer to perform causally masked, attention-weighted aggregation
of historical action signals into item representations, conditioned
on item similarity. As item embeddings propagate through succes-
sive layers, they evolve from encoding generic content semantics
(e.g., dog versus cat) to capturing user-conditioned semantics (e.g.,
preferred dog versus disfavored cat). Through this progressive inte-
gration, user preference signals are implicitly embedded into the

item representations, amplifying item–item contrast in a person-
alized manner. Notably, this personalization emerges end-to-end
from the attention mechanism itself, without requiring explicit user
profiling or handcrafted personalization features.
From a representation learning perspective,AttnMVPexplicitly
encodes the inductive bias that semantically related items elicit
analogous user responses. By decoupling item and action represen-
tations, the model circumvents the heterogeneous token entangle-
ment and quadratic computational overhead inherent in interleaved
generative frameworks. Consequently, AttnMVP offers a principled
and scalable alternative to token-level interleaving for sequential
behavioral modeling.

5 Future Work: AttnDHN - Attention based
Dual-Helix Network
Motivated by the strong empirical performance ofAttnMVP, we
further propose a symmetric dual-stream architecture, termed Attention-
based Dual-Helix Network(AttnDHN). InAttnMVP, item repre-
sentations are updated via self-attention with mixed item–action
values, using(𝑄𝑡,𝐾𝑡,𝑉𝑡)=(𝑖𝑡,𝑖𝑡,𝑖𝑡+𝑎𝑡).AttnDHNextends this
formulation by introducing a complementary action-centric up-
date, in which action representations are simultaneously refined

Figure 8. Within each Transformer block, item and action streams
are updated sequentially in a paired manner, forming a tightly cou-
pled interaction unit. This alternating update mechanism induces abidirectional flow of information between item and action repre-
sentations, analogous to a double-helix structure, enabling more
expressive and coherent co-evolution of user preference signals
across network depth.
To date, we do not observeAttnDHNto consistently outperform
AttnMVP. We attribute this outcome to three primary factors. First,
AttnDHNexhibits reduced training stability relative toAttnMVP;
in practice, stable optimization requires halving the learning rate.
When both models are trained for the same number of optimiza-
tion steps, this constraint leads to weaker convergence and inferior
performance forAttnDHN. Second,AttnDHNeffectively doubles
the number of Transformer updates per layer due to its dual-stream
design, making direct comparisons withAttnMVPless straight-
forward. Improvements observed at a fixed depth (e.g., 12 layers)
cannot be cleanly attributed to architectural superiority, as similar
gains might be achievable by increasing the depth ofAttnMVP.
Third, and more fundamentally, item and action tokens reside in
highly heterogeneous semantic spaces: the action vocabulary is
small (on the order of tens), whereas the item space is effectively
unbounded. As a result, action-centric representations tend to be
less expressive and noisier than item-centric representations (e.g.,
“preferred dog” versus a diffuse mixture of preferences over many
unrelated items).
Despite these limitations, we includeAttnDHNas an exploratory
architecture. Its symmetric dual-stream design may be better suited
to settings in which the two representation spaces are more ho-
mogeneous, such as multimodal recommendation scenarios that
jointly model text and visual embeddings. We leave a systematic
investigation of such applications to future work.

We revisit the interleaved-token formulation common in generative
recommendation and offer a first-principles critique of its opera-
tional mechanics. Our analysis reveals that while self-attention
effectively acts as a latent pooling mechanism for user actions via
item-level semantics, the standard interleaved approach remains
suboptimal. Specifically, this formulation introduces representa-
tional noise and computational inefficiency by interleaving hetero-
geneous tokens, which not only doubles sequence length but also
complicates the attention landscape.
Guided by the causal structure that an item interaction 𝑖𝑡induces
its corresponding user action 𝑎𝑡, we propose a family of attention-
based architectures that explicitly encode this causality without
interleaving. We introduceAttnLFA, which formulates action mod-
eling as causally masked attention-based late fusion, andAttnMVP,
which further generalizes this idea through mixed-value early fu-
sion that progressively integrates historical action information into
item representations. From an information-theoretic perspective,
these designs reduce attention noise by constraining aggregation
to causally valid and semantically aligned interactions, enabling
more efficient and expressive representation learning.
Empirically, both architectures consistently outperform a strong
interleaved ranker baseline on large-scale real-world recommen-
dation data, achieving lowerevaluation lossandnormalized
entropyacross major tasks while substantially reducing training
time and computational cost. These gains validate our central thesis:

structure.title: Beyond Interleaving: Causal Attention Reformulations for Generative Recommender Systems
structure.summary:
This partial document introduces a new approach to generative recommender systems that aims to overcome limitations of current "interleaving" methods. The main points covered are:

*   **Problem with Interleaving:** Current generative recommender systems (like Meta's HSTU) model user behavior by interleaving item and action tokens. This leads to several issues:
    *   Doubled sequence length.
    *   Quadratic computational overhead.
    *   Reliance on implicit attention to infer causal relationships (item interaction leading to an action).
    *   Attention noise and reduced representation efficiency due to forcing Transformers to process semantically incompatible item and action tokens.
*   **Proposed Solution:** The paper proposes a principled reformulation that aligns sequence modeling with causal structure and attention theory. It suggests that interleaving is an inefficient proxy for similarity-weighted action pooling.
*   **Novel Architectures:** Two new architectures are introduced:
    *   **Attention-based Late Fusion for Actions (AttnLFA):** Performs causal attention pooling over historical actions, conditioned on item similarity.
    *   **Attention-based Mixed Value Pooling (AttnMVP):** Integrates action signals earlier by mixing item and action embeddings in the Transformer's value stream, learning preference-aware item representations.
*   **Benefits of New Architectures:**
    *   Explicitly encode the causal dependency of an item interaction ($i_n$) eliciting a user action ($a_n$).
    *   Reduce sequence complexity by 50% by eliminating interleaved dependencies.
    *   Enforce strict causal attention while maintaining Transformer expressiveness.
    *   Theoretically grounded and computationally efficient.
    *   AttnMVP reduces attention noise by aligning the attention space with the true causal graph of user behavior.
*   **Experimental Results:** Evaluation on large-scale product recommendation data shows that AttnLFA and AttnMVP achieve consistent improvements in evaluation loss and normalized entropy gains compared to the interleaved baseline. They also reduce training time. Ablation studies confirm that early, causally constrained fusion of action signals is key to performance gains.
*   **Conclusion:** The work demonstrates that explicitly modeling item-action causality leads to more efficient, scalable, and accurate generative recommender systems, offering a new design paradigm beyond token interleaving.

nodes.title: Semantic Heterogeneity of Tokens
nodes.summary:
This document proposes a new approach to generative recommender systems that moves beyond the current "interleaving" method of modeling user behavior. The interleaving approach, used in systems like Meta's HSTU, treats user actions and item interactions as a single sequence, which leads to several problems:

*   **Increased Sequence Length and Computational Cost:** Doubling the sequence length leads to a four-fold increase in computational overhead due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention.
*   **Attention Noise and Inefficiency:** Interleaving heterogeneous item and action tokens forces Transformers to learn artificial relationships, creating attention noise and reducing representation efficiency.
*   **Lack of Explicit Causality:** The interleaving method implicitly models the causal relationship between an item interaction and a user action, but it doesn't explicitly enforce this causality, leading to diluted attention and structural ambiguity.

To address these limitations, the paper introduces two novel architectures:

*   **Attention-based Late Fusion for Actions (AttnLFA):** This method performs causal attention pooling over historical actions, conditioned on item similarity.
*   **Attention-based Mixed Value Pooling (AttnMVP):** This approach integrates action signals earlier by mixing item and action embeddings in the Transformer's value stream, leading to more preference-aware item representations.

These new architectures explicitly encode the causal dependency between items and actions, reduce sequence complexity by 50%, and enforce strict causal attention. The paper demonstrates through large-scale experiments that these methods achieve consistent improvements in evaluation loss and normalized entropy gains while significantly reducing training time compared to the interleaved baseline. The findings suggest that explicitly modeling item-action causality offers a more efficient, scalable, and accurate paradigm for generative recommender systems.

nodes.title: Missing Explicit Causality in Self-Attention
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses limitations of interleaved item-action sequence modeling in Transformer-based generative recommender (GR) models. It highlights issues such as:

*   **Missing Explicit Causality:** Interleaved sequences treat items and actions as homogeneous tokens, obscuring the direct causal dependency of an action on a specific item and introducing "attention noise." The model struggles to learn the asymmetric and causal relationship between items and actions.
*   **Causal Dilution and Structural Ambiguity:** Standard self-attention mechanisms cause action tokens to attend to the entire historical prefix, diluting the direct causal link to the current item. Item tokens also face difficulty mapping specific previous actions to their corresponding items.
*   **Attention Noise Induced by Interleaving:** The interleaved format creates spurious dependencies where later items might attend to earlier actions due to locality-preserving positional encodings, burdening subsequent layers.
*   **Computational Inefficiency:** Doubling the sequence length (from N items to 2N tokens) quadratically increases memory and computational costs, making interleaved models less scalable for large-scale systems.

The document then proposes a new formulation for GR models that addresses these limitations by reformulating the modeling as an attention pooling mechanism. It introduces two improved Transformer architectures that decouple item and action representations while preserving sequential dependencies, demonstrating improvements in recommendation accuracy and computational efficiency on large-scale product recommendation data. The proposed approach incorporates item features (content, metadata), personalization signals (viewer-side contextual features), and action features (user feedback signals).

nodes.title: Computational Inefficiency
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses limitations of current interleaved Transformer-based generative recommender (GR) systems, particularly concerning how they model item-action dependencies. The main points covered are:

*   **Implicit Assumptions and Weaknesses of Interleaving:** The interleaved format treats items and actions as a single token stream, implicitly assuming a shared latent structure. This is problematic because the relationship between an item and an action is causal and asymmetric, not compositional. This forces Transformers to learn artificial alignments.
*   **Missing Explicit Causality in Self-Attention:** Standard self-attention mechanisms in interleaved models suffer from "causal dilution" (actions attending to irrelevant history) and "structural ambiguity" (difficulty mapping specific actions to items). Positional encodings alone cannot fix this.
*   **Attention Noise Induced by Interleaving:** The interleaved structure leads to systematic attention noise, creating spurious dependencies (e.g., an item attending to a previous action it shouldn't) due to locality-preserving mechanisms like RoPE or RAB. This burdens subsequent layers and degrades efficiency.
*   **Computational Inefficiency:** Interleaving doubles the effective sequence length, leading to a four-fold increase in memory and computational cost due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. This is a significant drawback for large-scale systems.
*   **Proposed Solution:** The document introduces a new formulation for GR models that addresses these limitations by explicitly interpreting interleaving-based methods as attention pooling. They propose reformulating GR modeling as an attention pooling mechanism where item embeddings form queries/keys and action embeddings form values under strict causal masking.
*   **Improved Architectures:** Two improved Transformer architectures are introduced that decouple item and action representations while preserving sequential dependency. These models are evaluated on large-scale data and show improvements in accuracy and efficiency.
*   **Traditional GR Architecture and Features:** The document also describes the traditional interleaved GR architecture, including how item and action embeddings are generated and interleaved. It mentions the use of late-fusion features for score calibration and the importance of fine-grained semantic understanding for personalization, which sequence-based models aim to learn directly.
*   **Illustrative Toy Example:** A toy example with two users and contrasting preferences for dog and cat items is used to illustrate how personalized signals are learned from interaction sequences.

structure.title: Architecture overview and attention mechanism
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses generative recommender systems (GRs) and proposes a new architecture called AttnLFA (Attention-based Late Fusion for Action). The main points covered are:

*   **Traditional Interleaved GR Architecture:** It explains how standard Transformer-based GRs interleave item and action tokens (e.g., `[item0, action0, item1, action1, ...]`) before processing them through Transformer layers. This interleaving aims to implicitly learn user preferences and item-action dependencies from sequences.
*   **Limitations of Interleaving:** The document highlights several drawbacks of the interleaved approach:
    *   **Attention Noise:** Forcing heterogeneous item and action tokens into a single sequence leads to spurious interactions and representational noise, as the attention mechanism struggles to disentangle different semantic types. This can result in inaccurate predictions, like a "partially liked cat" example.
    *   **Computational Overhead:** Doubling the effective sequence length increases computational costs.
    *   **Prior Work Limitations:** It critiques existing attempts to mitigate these issues, such as early fusion and Lagged Action Conditioning (LAC), pointing out their limitations in terms of training complexity, distributional mismatch, and lack of semantic coherence.
*   **Proposed AttnLFA Architecture:** The core of the proposal is a new architecture that explicitly models the causal relationship between an exposed item and a subsequent user action.
    *   **Item-Conditioned Action Pooling:** Instead of interleaving, AttnLFA treats user actions as a similarity-weighted aggregation over historical actions. The idea is that if a target item is similar to previously consumed items, the user's response should resemble past actions on similar items.
    *   **Separate Representation Streams:** Item and action embeddings are maintained separately.
    *   **Attention Mechanism:** Contextualized item representations are used as Queries and Keys, while action embeddings serve as Values in an attention operation. This produces an item-conditioned pooled action representation.
    *   **Causal Constraint:** A strict causal constraint is enforced to prevent label leakage, ensuring that an item at position `n` can only attend to items at positions `{0, ..., n-1}`.
*   **Motivation:** The document argues that this new formulation preserves the benefits of learning item-action associations from sequences while avoiding the representational and computational drawbacks of interleaving.

nodes.title: AttnLFA: Attention-based Late Fusion for Action Architecture
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses advancements in generative recommender systems, focusing on how to effectively model user preferences and actions. It begins by analyzing the limitations of interleaved generative recommender architectures, where item and action tokens are mixed in a single sequence. The authors argue that this interleaving leads to "attention noise" and computational overhead due to the need to disentangle heterogeneous semantic types.

The document then introduces two novel architectures:

1.  **AttnLFA (Attention-based Late Fusion for Action Architecture):** This approach reformulates the recommendation problem as an item-conditioned action pooling task. It uses attention to explicitly model the causal relationship between an exposed item and a subsequent user action, avoiding the drawbacks of interleaving. AttnLFA separates item and action embeddings and uses a causally constrained attention mechanism to pool action representations based on item similarity. Experimental results show AttnLFA achieves superior predictive accuracy and reduced training time compared to a baseline interleaved model.

2.  **AttnMVP (Attention-based Mixed Value Pooling Architecture):** This is an early-fusion variant that builds upon AttnLFA. AttnMVP iteratively refines item representations by integrating historical user actions through attention-based value mixing within Transformer layers. This allows action signals to be progressively injected into item representations, enabling them to evolve from generic content semantics to user-conditioned semantics.

The document also details the experimental setup, including the dataset, evaluation protocol, and metrics used (Long Dwell, Contribution, Like), and presents comparative performance results in a table. The core contribution is a principled analysis of Transformer dynamics in recommendation and the proposal of new architectures that explicitly model item-action dependencies without the inefficiencies of token interleaving.

nodes.title: AttnMVP: Attention based Mixed Value Pooling Architecture
nodes.summary: This document discusses novel attention-based architectures for generative recommender systems, moving beyond traditional interleaved-token formulations. It introduces two main models: AttnLFA and AttnMVP. AttnLFA uses causally masked attention for late fusion of item and action representations, demonstrating improved predictive accuracy and reduced training time compared to a baseline. AttnMVP extends this with an early-fusion approach, integrating action information earlier into item representations through mixed-value pooling, leading to even greater performance gains. The document also explores AttnDHN, a dual-stream architecture, but notes its current limitations in training stability and expressiveness due to heterogeneous representation spaces. The core contribution is the explicit modeling of causality between item interactions and user actions to enhance recommendation performance and efficiency.

structure.title: Future Work: AttnDHN - Attention based Dual-Helix Network
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses advancements in generative recommender systems, moving beyond traditional interleaved token approaches. The main points covered are:

*   **AttnMVP (Attention-based Mixed-Value Projection):** A novel architecture that reformulates causal attention for generative recommendation. It explicitly encodes the inductive bias that semantically related items elicit analogous user responses by decoupling item and action representations. This avoids the computational overhead and token entanglement of interleaved methods.
*   **Empirical Evaluation of AttnMVP:** Table 2 and accompanying text demonstrate that AttnMVP significantly outperforms a baseline interleaved ranker in terms of evaluation loss and normalized entropy across various tasks, while also reducing training time.
*   **Contribution of Early Fusion:** An analysis of a variant of AttnMVP (AttnMVP-LFA) suggests that the majority of performance gains stem from the early, causally constrained integration of action signals into item representations, supporting the hypothesis that explicitly encoding preference-aware semantics is crucial.
*   **AttnDHN (Attention-based Dual-Helix Network):** A proposed symmetric dual-stream architecture that extends AttnMVP by introducing a complementary action-centric update alongside the item-centric update. This aims for a more expressive co-evolution of user preference signals.
*   **Challenges with AttnDHN:** The document notes that AttnDHN does not consistently outperform AttnMVP due to reduced training stability, increased computational complexity per layer, and the inherent heterogeneity between item and action semantic spaces.
*   **Critique of Interleaved-Token Formulation:** The document revisits and critiques the standard interleaved-token approach, highlighting its suboptimality due to representational noise and computational inefficiency.
*   **Proposed Causal Attention Architectures:** The authors introduce AttnLFA (late fusion) and AttnMVP (early fusion) as a family of attention-based architectures that explicitly encode causality without interleaving, leading to more efficient and expressive representation learning.
*   **Conclusion:** The document concludes that their proposed causal attention reformulations, particularly AttnMVP, offer a principled and scalable alternative to interleaved methods, achieving superior performance and efficiency in generative recommendation.

structure.title: Conclusion
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses advancements in generative recommender systems, moving beyond traditional "interleaving" methods. The main points covered are:

*   **Critique of Interleaved-Token Frameworks:** The document highlights the inefficiencies and representational noise introduced by interleaving item and action tokens in generative recommendation models.
*   **Causality-Aware Attention Reformulations:** It proposes new attention-based architectures that explicitly model the causal relationship between item interactions and user actions, without interleaving tokens.
*   **AttnMVP Model:** This model is introduced as a principled and scalable alternative. It encodes the inductive bias that semantically related items elicit analogous user responses by decoupling item and action representations. AttnMVP achieves significant improvements in evaluation loss, normalized entropy, and training time compared to a baseline interleaved ranker.
*   **Contribution of Early Fusion:** Experiments with a variant of AttnMVP (AttnMVP-LFA) suggest that the majority of performance gains stem from early, causally constrained integration of action signals into item representations.
*   **AttnDHN (Attention-based Dual-Helix Network):** This is an exploratory, symmetric dual-stream architecture proposed for future work. It aims to refine item and action representations simultaneously through a tightly coupled interaction unit. However, it faces challenges with training stability and semantic heterogeneity between item and action spaces in standard recommender settings.
*   **Overall Conclusion:** The document concludes that moving beyond interleaving towards causality-aware attention formulations offers a principled and scalable path forward for generative recommender systems, leading to improved predictive accuracy and system efficiency.

structure.title: Acknowledgments
structure.summary:
This partial document describes the Attention-based Dual-Helix Network (AttnDHN) architecture for generative recommender systems. Key points include:

*   **Architecture:** AttnDHN updates action and item embeddings in a pair-wise sequence within individual Transformer layers. Both layers use action/item embeddings as queries/keys and a combined item+action embedding as values.
*   **Causal Relationship Modeling:** The network explicitly models the causal relationship from items to actions, leading to improved predictive accuracy and system efficiency.
*   **Extension and Limitations:** A symmetric dual-stream extension, AttnDNA, is explored, with its limitations in standard recommender settings due to semantic heterogeneity highlighted. Its potential in more homogeneous multimodal scenarios is also noted.
*   **Future Direction:** The results suggest that causality-aware attention formulations are a promising path for generative recommender systems, moving beyond simple interleaving.
*   **Acknowledgments:** The author expresses gratitude for funding, support, guidance, discussions, and infrastructure support from various individuals and teams.
*   **References:** A list of 14 references is provided, covering topics such as deep learning for recommender systems, efficient attention mechanisms, generative recommendation frameworks, and transformer-based models.

structure.title: References
structure.summary:
This partial document describes an "Attention-based Dual-Helix Network (AttnDHN)" architecture for generative recommender systems. Key points include:

*   **Pair-wise Sequence Updates:** Action and item embeddings are updated in a paired sequence within individual Transformer layers.
*   **Query, Key, Value Mechanism:** Both Transformer layers utilize action and item embeddings as queries and keys, and a combined item+action embedding as the value.
*   **Causal Attention for Action Prediction:** Action embeddings are pooled using causally masked attention, conditioned on sequence-level item representations. The resulting pooled action representation is then fused with the final item embedding for action predictions.
*   **Causality Modeling:** The approach explicitly models the causal relationship from items to actions, leading to improved accuracy and system efficiency.
*   **AttnDNA Extension:** A symmetric dual-stream extension, AttnDNA, is explored, with its limitations in standard recommender settings due to semantic heterogeneity highlighted, and its potential in more homogeneous multimodal scenarios noted.
*   **Future Direction:** The results suggest that moving beyond interleaving to causality-aware attention formulations offers a principled and scalable path for generative recommender systems.
*   **Acknowledgments and References:** The document also includes acknowledgments for funding, support, guidance, and discussions, as well as a list of references to related research in recommender systems and deep learning.
